prompt: A seller installed a built-in dishwasher and now argues that it is personal property because two screws release it. Which analysis is most appropriate?

options.text: Consider attachment, adaptation, objective intention, the parties' relationship, and their agreement.
options.explanation: Fixture status depends on the circumstances as a whole; ease of removal alone does not settle the issue.

options.text: Treat any object removable with hand tools as personal property.
options.explanation: Many fixtures can be detached with ordinary tools. Removability is not the sole test.

options.text: Classify it according to its original purchase price.
options.explanation: Cost does not determine whether personal property has become part of the realty.

options.text: Accept the seller's undisclosed present intention as controlling.
options.explanation: Objective circumstances and the agreement matter; an uncommunicated later preference is not conclusive.

prompt: A commercial tenant installs business shelving. The tenant wants to remove it during the lease term without injuring the premises. What is the best starting point?

options.text: All shelving belongs to the landlord immediately upon installation.
options.explanation: Qualifying trade fixtures can remain removable; attachment alone does not resolve the tenant's rights.

options.text: Review trade fixture rules and the lease's removal and restoration terms.
options.explanation: California recognizes qualifying tenant removal rights, subject to statutory limits and the lease.

options.text: The tenant may remove any structural component used by the business.
options.explanation: Business use does not create an unlimited right to dismantle the premises.

options.text: The tenant must wait until after the tenancy ends to remove it.
options.explanation: The statutory rule addresses qualifying removal during the tenancy, not a universal right after expiration.

prompt: An owner lawfully cuts a tree and sells the detached logs. The change from an attached tree to movable logs illustrates:

options.text: Annexation.
options.explanation: Annexation attaches an item to real property; this scenario involves detachment.

options.text: An easement appurtenant.
options.explanation: An appurtenant easement is a use right benefiting land, not a change in an object's classification.

options.text: Severance.
options.explanation: Severance detaches an item from the realty, converting the detached item into personal property.

options.text: Subordination.
options.explanation: Subordination changes the priority of interests, not whether an object is attached.

prompt: An investor owns shares in a corporation that owns an apartment building. The investor's shares are generally:

options.text: A direct fee-simple interest in each apartment.
options.explanation: The corporation owns the real estate; share ownership is not direct title to each unit.

options.text: An easement over the building.
options.explanation: Shares are ownership interests in an entity, not rights to use a specified part of land.

options.text: A life estate in the land.
options.explanation: Nothing in share ownership creates an estate measured by a life.

options.text: Personal property representing an interest in the corporation.
options.explanation: The investor's asset is the stock, while the corporation separately owns the real property.

prompt: Two lots have identical dimensions but different locations. Which physical characteristic best explains why they are not identical real estate assets?

options.text: Nonhomogeneity.
options.explanation: Every parcel occupies a unique location, making land nonhomogeneous even when dimensions match.

options.text: Liquidity.
options.explanation: Liquidity concerns how readily an asset can be converted to cash, not its unique physical identity.

options.text: Depreciation.
options.explanation: Depreciation concerns loss in value or tax cost allocation; it does not define uniqueness.

options.text: Fungibility.
options.explanation: Fungibility means interchangeability; real parcels are not perfectly interchangeable.

prompt: A purchase agreement expressly includes a freestanding refrigerator that ordinarily would be personal property. What should the salesperson conclude?

options.text: Personal property can never be included in a real estate sale agreement.
options.explanation: The parties can agree to transfer personal property alongside the real estate.

options.text: The written inclusion makes transfer of the refrigerator part of the agreed transaction.
options.explanation: Express terms can specify what transfers, avoiding reliance only on default classifications.

options.text: The refrigerator must remain with the seller because it is unplugged.
options.explanation: Physical attachment does not override a clear contractual inclusion of personal property.

options.text: Its inclusion automatically makes every appliance a fixture.
options.explanation: The agreement concerns the identified item and does not reclassify all other appliances.

prompt: A deed grants Lee an estate for Lee's lifetime and then grants the property to Morgan. Morgan holds a:

options.text: Reversion.
options.explanation: A reversion is retained by the grantor; the future interest here is granted to another person.

options.text: Periodic tenancy.
options.explanation: Morgan's interest is not a tenancy renewing from period to period.

options.text: Remainder.
options.explanation: Morgan holds a future interest becoming possessory after the preceding life estate ends.

options.text: Lien.
options.explanation: A lien secures an obligation, while Morgan has a future ownership estate.

prompt: Two unrelated buyers take title as tenants in common, one with 70% and the other with 30%. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The larger owner has exclusive possession of 70% of the physical land.
options.explanation: Undivided shares do not automatically partition the parcel into exclusive physical areas.

options.text: Their shares must be converted to equal shares before the deed is valid.
options.explanation: Tenancy in common permits unequal ownership interests.

options.text: The survivor automatically receives the deceased owner's share.
options.explanation: Tenancy in common has no inherent survivorship right.

options.text: Each holds an undivided interest with rights of possession subject to the other's rights.
options.explanation: Co-owners share possessory rights in the whole property even when ownership percentages differ.

prompt: Three people own property in joint tenancy. One conveys that person's entire interest to an outsider. Assuming no other changes, what generally results?

options.text: The outsider holds as a tenant in common with the two owners, who retain joint tenancy between themselves.
options.explanation: The conveyance severs the transferring owner's joint tenancy interest, but need not destroy survivorship between the remaining joint tenants.

options.text: The outsider automatically becomes a joint tenant with full survivorship.
options.explanation: A transfer of one joint tenant's interest ordinarily severs that interest rather than automatically recreating joint tenancy.

options.text: The conveyance is impossible without unanimous consent.
options.explanation: A joint tenant can generally transfer that tenant's own interest.

options.text: The two remaining owners immediately acquire the transferred share.
options.explanation: Survivorship applies at death to an unsevered interest, not to a living owner's completed conveyance.

prompt: A married couple wants a California vesting form that expressly combines community property with survivorship. Which form addresses that request?

options.text: Tenancy in common.
options.explanation: Tenancy in common does not carry inherent survivorship.

options.text: Community property with right of survivorship.
options.explanation: Civil Code section 682.1 recognizes this expressly created community property form.

options.text: Severalty held by both spouses.
options.explanation: Severalty describes one owner, not concurrent title held by both spouses.

options.text: An estate at sufferance.
options.explanation: A tenancy at sufferance concerns holdover possession, not marital ownership vesting.

prompt: A corporation owns a residential building. A resident owns shares coupled with a proprietary lease. This most closely describes:

options.text: A condominium unit owned directly by the resident.
options.explanation: Condominium ownership generally includes a separate real property interest; this resident owns stock and an occupancy right.

options.text: A joint tenancy in the corporation's entire building.
options.explanation: Corporate shares do not automatically create direct joint tenancy in the corporation's assets.

options.text: A stock cooperative.
options.explanation: The corporation owns the real estate and stock ownership is coupled with the right to occupy.

options.text: A public utility easement.
options.explanation: A utility easement is a limited land-use right unrelated to this ownership structure.

prompt: A lease begins on January 1 and ends on September 30 of the same year. Its fixed duration is an example of:

options.text: A life estate.
options.explanation: A life estate is measured by a person's life, not a fixed calendar ending.

options.text: A month-to-month periodic tenancy.
options.explanation: This agreement has a stated final date rather than automatic monthly renewal.

options.text: A tenancy at sufferance from the first day.
options.explanation: Sufferance concerns holding over after a lawful right ends, not authorized possession under this lease.

options.text: An estate for years.
options.explanation: An estate for years has a definite duration and need not last a full year.

prompt: A rear parcel has a recorded driveway easement across a front parcel. The rear parcel is the:

options.text: Dominant tenement.
options.explanation: The rear parcel benefits from the appurtenant access right and is therefore dominant.

options.text: Servient tenement.
options.explanation: The front parcel bears the easement burden and is servient.

options.text: Lienholder.
options.explanation: An access benefit is not a monetary claim securing debt.

options.text: Licensee under a revocable afternoon permission.
options.explanation: The facts specify a recorded easement, not temporary informal permission.

prompt: A utility holds an easement to maintain power lines, and the benefit does not attach to a dominant parcel. The easement is most accurately described as:

options.text: An estate for years.
options.explanation: An estate for years is a possessory tenancy, not this limited utility right.

options.text: An easement in gross.
options.explanation: An easement in gross benefits a person or entity rather than a dominant parcel.

options.text: A mechanic's lien.
options.explanation: A mechanic's lien is a financial claim associated with qualifying improvement work.

options.text: A tenancy in common.
options.explanation: The utility has a limited use right, not an undivided ownership share in the entire parcel.

prompt: For six years, a neighbor has used a driveway with the owner's express permission. Which element of an ordinary prescriptive easement claim is most clearly absent?

options.text: Visibility.
options.explanation: Permitted use may be completely visible; permission does not make it hidden.

options.text: Passage of time.
options.explanation: Six years exceeds the ordinary five-year period, but duration alone is insufficient.

options.text: Adverse use.
options.explanation: Use with the owner's permission ordinarily lacks the adversity required for prescription.

options.text: A physical route.
options.explanation: The driveway supplies a route; the legal defect is the permissive nature of use.

prompt: Which statement correctly relates liens and encumbrances?

options.text: Every encumbrance secures repayment of money.
options.explanation: Easements and private use restrictions can be nonmonetary encumbrances.

options.text: A lien transfers full ownership to the creditor immediately.
options.explanation: A lien secures an obligation and does not itself give the creditor complete ownership.

options.text: An easement is always a general lien.
options.explanation: An easement is a use right, not automatically a debt-security claim.

options.text: All liens are encumbrances, but some encumbrances are not liens.
options.explanation: Liens are the monetary subset of a broader category of claims and burdens.

prompt: A lender with an earlier lien agrees that a later construction loan will have priority. The agreement is a:

options.text: Subordination agreement.
options.explanation: Subordination places one interest behind another in priority by agreement.

options.text: Merger of the dominant and servient tenements.
options.explanation: Merger concerns ownership of parcels or interests, not the stated priority agreement.

options.text: Prescription.
options.explanation: Prescription involves qualifying adverse use over time, not lender consent.

options.text: Novation of the property's legal description.
options.explanation: Novation substitutes a contractual obligation or party; it does not describe this lien-priority change.

prompt: A survey shows a neighbor's garage wall extends two feet over the boundary. The physical condition is an:

options.text: Automatic grant of fee-simple title.
options.explanation: A physical intrusion does not by itself establish that title has transferred.

options.text: Encroachment.
options.explanation: An encroachment is a physical intrusion onto another's property.

options.text: Ad valorem assessment.
options.explanation: An ad valorem assessment relates to value-based taxation, not a boundary intrusion.

options.text: Express easement by the surveyor.
options.explanation: A survey identifies physical and boundary evidence; it does not automatically grant an easement.

prompt: What is the nominal acreage of the east half of the northwest quarter of a section?

options.text: 40 acres.
options.explanation: Forty acres is one-sixteenth of a section; this description identifies one-eighth.

options.text: 160 acres.
options.explanation: One quarter contains 160 acres, but the description takes only half of that quarter.

options.text: 80 acres.
options.explanation: 640 acres multiplied by one-quarter and then one-half equals 80 acres.

options.text: 320 acres.
options.explanation: 320 acres is one half of an entire section, ignoring the quarter-section limitation.

prompt: A rectangular lot is 110 feet wide and 198 feet deep. How many acres does it contain?

options.text: 2 acres.
options.explanation: The lot contains 21,780 square feet, far less than the 87,120 square feet in two acres.

options.text: 1 acre.
options.explanation: One acre requires 43,560 square feet; this lot has half that area.

options.text: 0.25 acre.
options.explanation: One-quarter acre is 10,890 square feet, half of this lot's area.

options.text: 0.50 acre.
options.explanation: 110 multiplied by 198 equals 21,780 square feet; dividing by 43,560 gives 0.50 acre.

prompt: A description starts at an identified monument, follows several bearings and distances, and returns to its starting point. Which method is being used?

options.text: Metes and bounds.
options.explanation: The description traces a perimeter using boundary calls, directions, and distances.

options.text: An assessor's parcel number alone.
options.explanation: An APN is an assessment identifier and does not itself trace these boundary calls.

options.text: A gross rent multiplier.
options.explanation: A gross rent multiplier is a valuation ratio, not a land-description method.

options.text: A postal delivery designation.
options.explanation: Postal addresses locate deliveries rather than describing a survey traverse.

prompt: A seller provides a street address and an APN but no deed description. What is the sound conclusion?

options.text: The APN always proves the property is a legally created buildable lot.
options.explanation: Assessment identification does not guarantee legal lot status or development approval.

options.text: The identifiers help research, but the legal description and lot status require verification.
options.explanation: Addresses and APNs serve useful administrative purposes without automatically resolving title boundaries or legal lot status.

options.text: The address must identify every easement benefiting the property.
options.explanation: A street address does not enumerate appurtenant rights.

options.text: The salesperson should draw a new legal boundary using the listing photograph.
options.explanation: A photograph is not sufficient boundary evidence and does not authorize professional surveying.

prompt: A lot has 75 feet of street frontage and is offered at $2,400 per front foot. What is the indicated price?

options.explanation: Dividing the rate by a frontage figure does not produce the offered total price.
The frontage and per-foot rate must be multiplied, not added.
75 front feet multiplied by $2,400 per front foot equals $180,000.

options.text: The lot's depth must be known before this price can be calculated.
options.explanation: Depth is needed for rectangular area, but this stated price is based only on frontage.

prompt: A city imposes a lawful setback to protect safety and orderly development without acquiring the affected strip. This is primarily an exercise of:

options.text: Escheat.
options.explanation: Escheat concerns property without a legally entitled owner or successor, not a setback.

options.text: Eminent domain in every case.
options.explanation: An ordinary lawful setback is regulation; not every reduction in usable area is a compensable taking.

options.text: Private deed restriction enforcement.
options.explanation: The restriction here comes from a city regulation rather than a private covenant.

options.text: Police power.
options.explanation: Police power supports land-use regulation for legitimate public purposes.

prompt: An agency uses a legal proceeding to acquire private land for a public road with required compensation. The proceeding is called:

options.text: Condemnation.
options.explanation: Condemnation is the legal process exercising eminent domain.

options.text: Escheat.
options.explanation: Escheat does not describe acquisition from an identified private owner for a road.

options.text: A conditional use permit.
options.explanation: A conditional use permit approves a use under zoning; it does not acquire private title.

options.text: A restrictive covenant.
options.explanation: A covenant is a private restriction or obligation, not this governmental acquisition process.

prompt: An unusually shaped lot cannot meet the ordinary side-yard requirement. Its owner seeks qualifying property-specific relief without adding a prohibited use. The owner is most likely seeking:

options.text: A general plan for the entire county.
options.explanation: A general plan establishes broad policy; it is not individualized relief from a setback.

options.text: A variance.
options.explanation: A variance can address qualifying special property circumstances within statutory limits.

options.text: Escheat of neighboring land.
options.explanation: The owner's difficulty does not make neighboring property ownerless.

options.text: A guarantee that any requested development must be approved.
options.explanation: Special circumstances do not eliminate required findings or other development rules.

prompt: A lawful workshop use existed before a zoning change that no longer permits new workshops. The existing use may be a:

options.text: Use made lawful solely because no one complained.
options.explanation: The facts establish prior legality; lack of complaints alone would not legalize an originally unlawful use.

options.text: Mandatory immediate public acquisition.
options.explanation: A zoning change does not automatically require government purchase of every affected property.

options.text: Legal nonconforming use subject to the governing continuation rules.
options.explanation: A use lawful when established may continue under limits imposed by applicable nonconforming-use rules.

options.text: Permanent exemption from every future safety regulation.
options.explanation: Nonconforming status does not create unlimited immunity from safety or continuation requirements.

prompt: Valid zoning allows a 30-foot building, but an enforceable recorded private covenant allows only 22 feet. No overriding statute invalidates the covenant. What height satisfies both stated limits?

options.text: 30 feet because public permission automatically cancels private restrictions.
options.explanation: Zoning permission does not ordinarily extinguish an independent enforceable covenant.

options.text: 26 feet because the limits must be averaged.
options.explanation: Legal restrictions are not resolved by averaging their numbers.

options.text: Any height the seller verbally approves.
options.explanation: A seller's informal approval does not necessarily modify zoning or a recorded covenant.

options.text: 22 feet.
options.explanation: A 22-foot building satisfies both the public maximum and the stricter enforceable private maximum.

prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes California's principal subdivision frameworks?

options.text: The Map Act primarily concerns local regulation of land division, while DRE's Subdivided Lands Law addresses covered offerings and buyer protection.
options.explanation: The frameworks have different purposes and administrators, even though both can apply to a development.

options.text: A DRE public report guarantees investment profit.
options.explanation: A public report provides required disclosures; it does not guarantee economic results.

options.text: Local map approval replaces every required DRE public report.
options.explanation: Local land-division approval does not eliminate independent offering requirements.

options.text: CEQA requires a full environmental impact report for every resale of a house.
options.explanation: CEQA concerns covered public-agency project decisions and includes exemptions and other review outcomes.

prompt: An owner claims an unlimited right to pump a well because the well is physically on the owner's land. What is the best response?

options.text: Land ownership guarantees unlimited groundwater extraction.
options.explanation: Groundwater rights remain subject to reasonable use, other rights, and applicable management rules.

options.text: Review the water right, reasonable-use limits, basin rules, and applicable local or state requirements.
options.explanation: Physical well ownership does not resolve the legal amount, place, or conditions of extraction.

options.text: Every well requires the identical permit used for a new surface-water appropriation.
options.explanation: Ordinary groundwater and surface-water permitting are not governed identically.

options.text: SGMA automatically transferred every private parcel to the state.
options.explanation: SGMA concerns groundwater management and does not transfer all underlying land ownership.

prompt: Which statement best describes a typical riparian surface-water right in California?

options.text: It permits unlimited export to any other land the owner buys.
options.explanation: Riparian use is tied to qualifying riparian land and is not an unrestricted export right.

options.text: It must be exercised every year or is automatically lost.
options.explanation: Riparian rights generally are not lost simply through nonuse.

options.text: It concerns reasonable use of natural flow on qualifying land adjoining the watercourse.
options.explanation: The right relates to the land's riparian character and remains subject to reasonable-use limits.

options.text: It is identical to ownership of the entire river.
options.explanation: A use right is not ownership of all water and river interests.

prompt: During a single flood, a river abruptly abandons its old channel and cuts a new one. This sudden change is:

options.text: Accretion.
options.explanation: Accretion is a gradual addition of soil, not an abrupt channel change.

options.text: Reliction.
options.explanation: Reliction generally concerns gradual exposure of land as water recedes.

options.text: Annexation.
options.explanation: Annexation in fixture analysis is attachment of an item to realty.

options.text: Avulsion.
options.explanation: Avulsion describes sudden, perceptible water-caused change and can have different boundary effects from gradual change.

prompt: A covered sale involves a home built in 1965. Which statement about the federal lead disclosure framework is most accurate?

options.text: It generally requires specified information and disclosures, with a buyer inspection opportunity subject to permitted agreement or waiver.
options.explanation: Covered pre-1978 housing is subject to known-hazard and report disclosures and the applicable inspection-opportunity rules.

options.text: The seller must always remove every trace of lead before any sale.
options.explanation: The disclosure rule is not a universal pre-sale lead-removal mandate.

options.text: A visual walk-through conclusively establishes whether lead is present.
options.explanation: Lead cannot reliably be ruled out by an ordinary visual inspection.

options.text: The rules apply only to buildings constructed after 1978.
options.explanation: The general federal target is most covered housing built before 1978, subject to exemptions.

prompt: A buyer plans to subdivide agricultural land that is subject to a Williamson Act contract. Which conclusion is appropriate?

options.text: The sale automatically cancels the contract.
options.explanation: A transfer does not automatically eliminate the land-use commitment.

options.text: The contract and applicable procedures must be reviewed because they can restrict nonagricultural development.
options.explanation: Williamson Act contracts exchange qualifying use restrictions for assessment treatment and affect development plans.

options.text: The contract guarantees local approval of residential lots.
options.explanation: The program does not provide a subdivision approval guarantee.

options.text: The contract proves the property has unlimited water rights.
options.explanation: Agricultural land-use status does not establish an unlimited legal water supply.

prompt: A purchase agreement includes an attached security camera owned by the seller. The buyer assumes the seller's paid monitoring account also transfers. Which conclusion is best?

options.text: An account can transfer only if the camera is personal property.
options.explanation: Service transfer depends on the contract, not solely on real-versus-personal property classification.

options.text: The equipment inclusion does not by itself establish transferability of the separate service account.
options.explanation: The physical asset and related contractual service can involve different rights; the service terms require separate verification.

options.text: Every service associated with a fixture transfers automatically.
options.explanation: Fixture classification does not override a service provider's contract or establish account transferability.

options.text: The monitoring service is included unless the seller expressly excludes it from the equipment clause.
options.explanation: A physical-equipment inclusion does not create a default transfer of a separate service contract; the account terms must be checked.

prompt: A farmer contracts to sell growing crops that the parties agree will be severed under the sale contract. Which distinction is most relevant?

options.text: The agreed severance can make the goods-sale treatment relevant despite present attachment.
options.explanation: The contract's treatment and the statutory severance provision matter; attachment alone does not answer this transaction.

options.text: Goods-sale treatment cannot apply until every crop has already been physically harvested.
options.explanation: The statute addresses certain crops and items agreed to be severed, so physical harvesting need not be completed before the sale agreement.

options.text: The severance agreement also converts the underlying land into personal property.
options.explanation: The agreed sale of specified crops does not reclassify or convey the underlying real estate.

options.text: All attached crops must remain real property for every sales-law purpose.
options.explanation: California's property classification statute addresses certain crops and items agreed to be severed for sale.

prompt: A landlord sells a building occupied by a nursery tenant. The tenant owns movable merchandise displayed inside. The building sale agreement does not include that merchandise. What is the sound conclusion?

options.text: The inventory transfers unless the tenant recorded ownership with the county recorder.
options.explanation: A tenant's ownership of movable merchandise does not depend on recording a real-property instrument to prevent the landlord from conveying it.

options.text: The inventory transfers because the buyer succeeds to the landlord's interest in the lease.
options.explanation: Acquiring the landlord's interest does not itself convey the tenant's separately owned merchandise.

options.text: The tenant's movable inventory does not transfer merely because the landlord sells the building.
options.explanation: The tenant's goods are a distinct asset, and the landlord's sale does not automatically convey them.

options.text: Commercial use converts all of the tenant's merchandise into trade fixtures belonging to the building owner.
options.explanation: Movable inventory does not automatically become a fixture, and trade-fixture rules do not make all tenant goods the landlord's property.

prompt: Two houses have identical solar panels. On one, the seller owns the equipment; on the other, the seller leases it from a third party. Why should a buyer investigate before treating the systems as equivalent?

options.text: Panel count conclusively determines the rights conveyed.
options.explanation: Identical physical equipment can be subject to different ownership and payment arrangements.

options.text: The ownership and lease obligations can materially change the interest and continuing costs acquired.
options.explanation: The buyer must evaluate equipment ownership, transfer requirements, and any ongoing obligations rather than only appearance.

options.text: The lease can be ignored because identical panels necessarily produce identical ownership costs.
options.explanation: A leased system can carry payment and transfer obligations that a seller-owned system does not.

options.text: The equipment's attachment makes the buyer a party to the existing lease without any need to review it.
options.explanation: Physical attachment does not settle contractual transfer requirements or establish the buyer's agreed obligations.

prompt: Nora holds an estate measured by Luis's life and conveys her entire interest to Priya. Nora later dies while Luis is alive. What generally determines the duration of Priya's interest?

options.text: Priya's life replaces Luis's life as the measure because Priya is the new holder.
options.explanation: A conveyance of the existing estate changes its holder, not the measuring life specified in the original grant.

options.text: Nora's death necessarily terminates it.
options.explanation: The estate was expressly measured by Luis's life rather than Nora's.

options.text: Luis's life remains the measuring life.
options.explanation: Priya receives the estate Nora held; the transfer does not change the designated measuring life.

options.text: Priya's purchase converts it to an unlimited fee simple.
options.explanation: A holder cannot enlarge a life estate merely by selling it.

prompt: Tenants in common own 50%, 30%, and 20% of a property sold for $900,000. Before costs, debts, or accounting adjustments, what gross proceeds correspond to the 30% share?

options.explanation: That is 70% of the sale price, the complementary percentage rather than the owner's 30% share.
That amount corresponds to the 20% interest, not the 30% interest.

options.text: $300,000 because there are three owners.
options.explanation: An equal division would disregard the stated unequal ownership shares.
Thirty percent of $900,000 is $270,000, before the adjustments excluded by the question.

prompt: A condominium advertisement calls a fenced patio 'private.' The recorded plan identifies it as exclusive-use common area. Which interpretation is most accurate?

options.text: Exclusive use proves the association has no possible role in maintenance.
options.explanation: Use and maintenance responsibilities must be determined from governing documents and law.

options.text: The word private automatically changes it to a separate fee-simple parcel.
options.explanation: Marketing language does not override the recorded ownership structure.

options.text: The patio can be treated as a separately owned parcel because its area appears on the marketing floor plan.
options.explanation: A marketing floor plan does not override the recorded definition of common area and exclusive-use rights.

options.text: Exclusive use and separate ownership are different; the recorded documents define the interest.
options.explanation: An area can be common area while assigned for exclusive use by a particular owner.

prompt: A shareholder dies owning shares in a corporation that holds title to a warehouse. Assuming no separate conveyance, what asset is the subject of succession from the shareholder?

options.text: An undivided warehouse interest equal to the shareholder's percentage of corporate stock.
options.explanation: A shareholder's percentage in the entity is not automatically a corresponding direct tenancy-in-common interest in each corporate asset.

options.text: A proprietary lease to the warehouse automatically created by ordinary corporate share ownership.
options.explanation: A proprietary occupancy lease can exist in a cooperative arrangement, but ordinary ownership of shares does not automatically create one.

options.text: Direct fee title to every portion of the warehouse.
options.explanation: The corporation, a separate owner, holds the real estate; the shareholder owns shares.

options.text: The shareholder's corporate shares.
options.explanation: Succession concerns the decedent's entity interest while the corporation continues to own its assets.

prompt: A valid shared-road maintenance agreement allocates 60% of repair costs to Parcel A and 40% to Parcel B. For a covered $12,000 repair, what is Parcel A's stated share?

options.explanation: The agreement's 60% allocation produces $12,000 multiplied by 0.60, or $7,200.

options.text: Nothing, because an easement conveys no maintenance obligations.
options.explanation: Private access rights can carry maintenance obligations under agreement and applicable law.
That is Parcel B's 40% share.

options.text: $6,000 because each owner holds one parcel.
options.explanation: Equal parcel count does not override the stated maintenance agreement.

prompt: A buyer discovers a recorded lis pendens arising from an ownership lawsuit. What does that document principally signal?

options.text: A title-insurance commitment guaranteeing that the disputed claim has been resolved.
options.explanation: A litigation notice does not resolve the claim or guarantee title insurance against it.

options.text: Pending litigation asserts a qualifying claim affecting the property.
options.explanation: A lis pendens provides notice of a pending real property claim and can affect the buyer's title analysis.

options.text: A monetary lien that fixes the claimant's dollar recovery before judgment.
options.explanation: A notice of pending action identifies qualifying litigation; it does not itself establish a fixed monetary award.

options.text: The claimant has already won a final judgment granting title.
options.explanation: Notice of pending litigation does not itself prove the claimant has prevailed.

prompt: A simplified distribution has $500,000 available after superior costs. A first-priority claim is $420,000 and a junior claim is $120,000. Under the stated priorities, how much remains for the junior claim?

options.text: $120,000 because every lien is fully paid before any shortfall occurs.
options.explanation: The available amount cannot fully cover both claims after the senior claim is satisfied.

options.text: $250,000 because the two lienholders split equally.
options.explanation: Priority, not equal division by creditor count, controls the assumed distribution.
$500,000 minus the $420,000 first-priority claim leaves $80,000.

options.text: $380,000 because the junior claim is deducted first.
options.explanation: That reverses the stated order of priority.

prompt: A recorded express driveway easement has not been used for two years. The buyer sees tall grass and assumes the right ended. Which response is best?

options.text: Investigate legally effective termination; mere nonuse ordinarily does not extinguish an express easement.
options.explanation: A release, abandonment under applicable law, or another termination basis must be distinguished from temporary nonuse.

options.text: Vegetation conclusively proves legal abandonment.
options.explanation: A physical condition alone does not establish the required legal basis for termination.

options.text: Any express easement expires after one unused year.
options.explanation: There is no general one-year nonuse expiration for express easements.

options.text: The buyer can disregard the recorded easement if the seller's disclosure form omits it.
options.explanation: Omission from a disclosure does not extinguish an existing easement or replace title investigation.

prompt: A 100-by-150-foot lot has a 9,200-square-foot setback envelope. A separate stated rule limits building coverage to 40% of lot area. With no exceptions, what is the maximum coverage allowed by the percentage rule?

options.text: 3,680 square feet.
options.explanation: That applies 40% to the envelope, while the stated rule uses total lot area.

options.text: 6,000 square feet.
options.explanation: Lot area is 15,000 square feet, and 40% of that area is 6,000 square feet.

options.text: 9,200 square feet.
options.explanation: That is the envelope area and ignores the separate, smaller coverage allowance.

options.text: 15,000 square feet.
options.explanation: That is total lot area before the stated coverage limit.

prompt: A deed conveys a nominal five-acre tract except a separately described 66-by-165-foot parcel. What nominal acreage is conveyed?

options.text: 5.25 acres.
options.explanation: The exception must be subtracted, not added.

options.text: 4 acres.
options.explanation: The exception is one-quarter acre, not one acre.

options.text: 4.75 acres.
options.explanation: The exception contains 10,890 square feet, or 0.25 acre; five minus 0.25 equals 4.75 acres.

options.text: 5 acres because every boundary burden leaves acreage unchanged.
options.explanation: A deed exception excludes land; it is different from a mere use easement burdening retained fee acreage.

prompt: A conveyance includes two nonoverlapping pieces: the west half of the southeast quarter of a section and the northeast quarter of that southeast quarter. What is their combined nominal acreage?

options.text: 120 acres.
options.explanation: The first piece is 80 acres and the second is 40 acres; their stated nonoverlapping total is 120 acres.

options.text: 320 acres.
options.explanation: That would be half of an entire section and ignores the smaller nested fractions.

options.text: 40 acres.
options.explanation: That counts only the quarter-of-a-quarter piece.

options.text: 80 acres.
options.explanation: That counts only the half-of-a-quarter piece.

prompt: A triangular parcel has a base of 120 feet and a perpendicular height of 80 feet. What is its area?

options.text: 4,800 square feet.
options.explanation: One-half multiplied by 120 feet and 80 feet equals 4,800 square feet.

options.text: 24,000 square feet.
options.explanation: No stated dimensions support this product; triangle area uses one-half times base times perpendicular height.

options.text: 200 square feet.
options.explanation: Adding the dimensions does not calculate an area.

options.text: 9,600 square feet.
options.explanation: That is base times height without the one-half factor required for a triangle.

prompt: A stated zoning rule allows four dwellings per acre on a two-acre site. Other development approvals have not been reviewed. What can be concluded from this rule alone?

options.text: The density calculation allows up to eight units, but other requirements may limit the project.
options.explanation: Four times two gives eight under the density rule; it does not establish satisfaction of every other development standard.

options.text: Eight units are guaranteed approval regardless of access or setbacks.
options.explanation: A density ceiling does not resolve independent development requirements.

options.text: Only two units are allowed because acreage controls without the stated rate.
options.explanation: The rule is four units per acre, not one unit per acre.

options.text: Eight separately saleable legal lots already exist because eight units fit the density calculation.
options.explanation: Permitted density does not itself create legal parcels or satisfy subdivision requirements.

prompt: An owner seeks a variance solely to open a retail store where the zoning does not authorize that use. The owner shows that the store would be profitable. Which answer best applies California's general variance rule?

options.text: The owner qualifies for relief by showing that retail would produce more income than residential use.
options.explanation: A more profitable use does not itself authorize a prohibited use through a variance or supply the required statutory findings.

options.text: The request is automatically a conditional use permit even though zoning does not conditionally authorize retail.
options.explanation: A conditional use permit concerns uses contemplated conditionally by the applicable zoning framework; the applicant cannot create that authorization by relabeling the request.

options.text: Profitability automatically supplies every required variance finding.
options.explanation: Financial desirability is not a substitute for the statutory property-specific basis and limits.

options.text: A variance cannot simply authorize an otherwise prohibited use under the general statute.
options.explanation: California's general variance provision does not permit granting a use that the zoning regulation does not expressly authorize.

prompt: A homeowners association approves a proposed addition, but the addition violates an applicable public building requirement. No exemption applies. What follows?

options.text: The association's approval proves the addition already has a building permit.
options.explanation: Approval by one body does not establish that another authority has issued its required approval.

options.text: The public requirement applies only if a neighbor objects.
options.explanation: Enforceability does not depend solely on a private complaint.

options.text: Association approval overrides the public requirement.
options.explanation: Private architectural approval does not generally excuse violation of public building law.

options.text: The owner must also satisfy the applicable public requirement.
options.explanation: Private approval and public compliance are independent layers of the development analysis.

prompt: Planning staff express informal support for a buyer's sketch, but no required permit has been issued. How should an agent describe the status?

options.text: Approval is final once the buyer pays the application fee.
options.explanation: Payment of a fee does not establish that the required agency findings or permit issuance have occurred.

options.text: Fully approved because staff liked the proposal.
options.explanation: Informal support is not equivalent to issuance of the required approval.

options.text: A proposal with informal staff support, subject to the remaining required approvals.
options.explanation: This accurately distinguishes encouragement from a completed approval process.

options.text: The buyer can safely remove approval contingencies because a staff comment binds every reviewing authority.
options.explanation: Informal staff support does not guarantee all required approvals or bind independent reviewing bodies.

prompt: A buyer's crop plan requires 60 acre-feet annually, but the documented entitlement permits 45 acre-feet under its terms. A well can physically pump more. What is the central unresolved issue?

options.text: The intended irrigation demand controls the entitlement because the use is agricultural.
options.explanation: A desired beneficial use does not independently enlarge the documented quantity or terms of an existing right.

options.text: A sufficiently large pump automatically expands the water right.
options.explanation: Equipment capacity does not override the terms and limits of the legal right.

options.text: Physical pumping capacity does not supply the missing legal entitlement.
options.explanation: Mechanical capacity and lawful water use are separate questions; the 15-acre-foot entitlement gap remains.

options.text: Owning agricultural land guarantees all water needed for any crop.
options.explanation: Land use and crop needs do not establish unlimited water rights.

prompt: A seller promises to reimburse the buyer for environmental cleanup costs. The buyer assumes this prevents any government claim against the buyer. What is the best conclusion?

options.text: Only the party that physically spilled a substance can ever face liability.
options.explanation: Environmental liability can extend to qualifying owners and other responsible parties, subject to law and protections.

options.text: The contract may allocate costs between the parties without eliminating the buyer's possible statutory responsibility.
options.explanation: Private reimbursement rights and liability to regulators are separate legal issues.

options.text: Any indemnity automatically eliminates liability under environmental statutes.
options.explanation: A private risk-allocation promise does not necessarily bar claims imposed by public law.

options.text: The promise proves the site contains no contamination.
options.explanation: An indemnity allocates risk; it is not evidence that an environmental condition is absent.

prompt: An owner imports fill to extend a shoreline and claims new title on the theory of natural accretion. Which response is best?

options.text: A photograph of the new shore is sufficient to amend the deed.
options.explanation: A photograph documents appearance but does not itself create or amend property rights.

options.text: Imported fill is legally identical to every gradual natural deposit.
options.explanation: The artificial cause matters and cannot simply be treated as natural accretion.

options.text: Any increase in dry surface automatically transfers public shoreline title.
options.explanation: Physical filling does not automatically establish ownership or defeat public trust interests.

options.text: The artificial filling does not itself establish new title; boundaries, permits, and public rights require review.
options.explanation: Creating dry ground is different from proving the legal effect of natural shoreline change.

prompt: A private owner grants a conservation easement restricting development but retains fee title. Which statement best describes the result?

options.text: The owner may disregard the restriction because possession remains private.
options.explanation: Retaining ownership does not eliminate the granted enforceable limitation.

options.text: Ownership continues subject to the granted conservation restriction.
options.explanation: A restriction on use and a transfer of complete ownership are distinct legal results.

options.text: No restriction exists unless the land is sold outright.
options.explanation: A conservation easement can restrict use without a fee conveyance.

options.text: The entire fee necessarily transfers to the easement holder.
options.explanation: The facts specify that the owner retains fee title while granting a limited interest.
